opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that a lot of it is less about exotic mathematics and more about getting the details right. Conceptually, a sparse mixture of experts is quite simple: instead of having every token go through every parameter of the network, you have a router that decides, for each token, which subset of experts should process it. So you get a model that has a lot of parameters in total, but only uses a fraction of them for any given token. That changes the trade-off between capacity and compute, which is really what you care about when you're thinking about scaling.

The hard part is that you're introducing a discrete decision into something you want to train with gradient descent. The routing is essentially a choice, and choices aren't naturally differentiable, so you have to think carefully about how gradients flow through the router and how you keep training stable. One of the classic failure modes is load imbalance: the router learns to send most tokens to a few experts, those experts get better, so the router sends them even more tokens, and you end up with a handful of overworked experts and many that do nothing. So a lot of the work is around balancing, through auxiliary losses and through how you set up the routing, so that the experts actually specialize and the capacity you've paid for gets used.

Then there's the systems side, which in practice is just as important as the math. When experts are spread across many accelerators, you have to move tokens to wherever their expert lives and then bring them back, so communication becomes a real bottleneck. You have to think about memory, about batching, and about how you serve these models efficiently at inference time, because the whole point is that you're getting more quality for a given inference cost. If the serving is inefficient, you lose the benefit.

The way we approached it was very empirical. You form hypotheses, run many smaller-scale experiments, look at scaling behavior, and only then commit compute to the bigger runs. A lot of the knowledge in this field is not written in papers; it's in knowing which hyperparameters matter, which instabilities to watch for, and how to read your training curves. Having a small team that had done this before and could iterate quickly was, I think, our biggest advantage.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the first thing to say is that sparse mixture-of-experts is not really a new mathematical object. The ideas go back to the nineties, and the Shazeer paper in 2017 showed you could make it work at scale. What changed for us was that we had a very practical constraint: we had limited compute, and we wanted a model that was as good as something much larger at inference cost. So the math we cared about was less about proving new theorems and more about making the routing stable and the load balanced during training.

The core problem is the router. You have a token, you compute a gate over, say, eight experts, you pick the top two, and you send the token there. That selection is discrete, so you don't get gradients through the choice itself. You only get gradients through the weights of the experts you picked and through the softmax scores. That makes the system very easy to collapse: a few experts become slightly better early on, they get picked more, they get more gradient, and you end up with two experts doing all the work and six that are dead. So a lot of the work was on the auxiliary losses that penalize imbalance, and on how strongly you weight them. Too strong and you hurt the model quality, too weak and you get collapse. We spent a lot of time looking at the distribution of tokens per expert over the course of training, almost as an observability problem rather than a theoretical one.

The second piece is systems math, which is honestly where most of the effort went. With a dense model you know exactly how much compute each layer uses. With MoE you have a capacity factor: each expert can only process so many tokens per batch before you have to drop or overflow. So you're doing this constant tradeoff between dropping tokens, which hurts quality, and padding, which wastes compute. And when you shard experts across GPUs, you have an all-to-all communication step that scales badly if you're not careful. So the "mathematical" question becomes: given my interconnect bandwidth and my batch size, what expert count and capacity factor actually gets me good hardware utilization. That's not elegant math, it's arithmetic and profiling, but getting it wrong costs you more than getting the architecture slightly wrong.

And the last thing, which people underestimate, is that the scaling laws change. The Chinchilla-style relationship between parameters, tokens, and loss doesn't transfer directly, because you now have active parameters and total parameters as separate quantities. We found you need to think about it as the active parameter count setting your compute budget, and the total count setting something like your knowledge capacity, and then you fit curves to that. We ran small experiments at a few scales to make sure the thing we were extrapolating was actually behaving like we thought before committing the full run.

So, to summarize: very little of it was deep mathematics in the academic sense. It was mostly being disciplined about stability, balance, and hardware, and being empirical enough to check your assumptions at small scale before you spend the money.

astra-6.text:
The central question is how to increase the capacity of the model without increasing the computation for every token by the same amount. With a mixture of experts, you have several sets of parameters, but you activate only a small subset for each token.

That introduces a routing problem. You learn which experts to send each token to, but you also need to keep the workload reasonably balanced. If the router sends everything to the same expert, you lose the benefit of the architecture. If you impose too much balance, you can interfere with what the model is learning. So there’s a tradeoff between letting the routing emerge and keeping training efficient and stable.

And the mathematics is tightly connected to the systems problem. Activating fewer parameters doesn’t automatically make the model faster, because you have to move tokens between devices. So the approach is to work on the architecture, the training objective, and the implementation together, then test whether the gains actually hold as you scale.

sol-6.1.text:
The way we approached it was quite empirical. With a mixture of experts, you have a routing mechanism that selects which parts of the model to activate for each token. So you’re increasing the total capacity without increasing the computation by the same amount. But then you have to make that routing work: you don’t want all the tokens going to the same expert, and you want the training to remain stable.

There’s also a systems problem intertwined with the mathematical problem. An architecture can look very efficient in terms of operations, but if it requires too much communication between devices, you lose that advantage. So you have to design the model and the way you distribute it together.

It’s really an iteration between hypotheses, smaller experiments, and scaling. The mathematics gives you a way to reason about the tradeoffs, but the experiments tell you whether those tradeoffs actually work.
